authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Rose 1.5x While Farmland Stayed Concentrated
authored_explainer.hook: Food fears missed this: cereal production rose 1.5x since 1972.
says: Progression to secondary school (%) rose from 77.8 in 1985 to 91.3 in 2017—1.2 times higher.
Cereal production climbed from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 million metric tons in 2024—1.5 times higher.
Farmland spans 5.2 million square kilometers in China, 4.2 million in the United States, 3.6 million Australia, 2.4 million Brazil, and 2.2 million Russia.
authored_explainer.closing: More food and schooling matter, but farmland control still shapes who benefits.
authored_explainer.question: Which shift surprised you most?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Tripled 3.0x, But Its Methane Problem Grew Too
authored_explainer.hook: Waste energy hit 3.0x its 1990 share—and emissions followed.
says: Combustible renewables and waste rose from 10.2 % of total energy in 1990 to 30.1 % of total energy in 2024—3.0 times higher.
Access to electricity rose from 73.2 % of population in 1998 to 91.9 % of population in 2024—1.3 times higher.
Methane (ch4) emissions from waste rose from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 Mt CO2e in 2024—1.8 times higher.
authored_explainer.closing: Turning waste into energy helps, but rising methane can erase part of the gain.
authored_explainer.question: Is waste power worth the tradeoff?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54%, Yet Cities Kept Expanding
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth fell 54%, but urban concentration barely moved.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1 % of total population in 1972 to 42.2 % of total population in 2025—down to 67 percent of that.
Population in the largest city shifted from 18.2 % of urban population in 1972 to 16.2 % of urban population in 2025—it barely moved.
Population growth fell from 2 annual % in 1972 to 0.91 annual % in 2025—down to 46 percent of that.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth changes schools, housing, and workforces long before population actually shrinks.
authored_explainer.question: Would your city feel this slowdown?
